newsitem.title: USA: Drillers reap benefits of booming oil spending.
newsitem.headline: Drillers reap benefits of booming oil spending.

text.p: The huge expansion in oil and gas exploration worldwide has produced better than expected second quarter earnings for offshore drilling contractors and with $1.5 trillion to be spent through 2005, demand for rigs is set to boom.

Between 1985 and 1995, just $330 billion was spent to find new oil and gas assets, but that started to turn in 1996, when oil majors spent more on exploration and production than they had done for a decade.

On Thursday, Marine Drilling Cos joined the list of companies exceeding expectations, with second quarter earnings per share of $0.26, compared with analysts's forecasts of $0.24 and $0.10 a year ago.
The company attributed the record quarter to 100 percent utilsation of its offshore fleet and an eight percent rise in the rate oil companies are prepared to pay for its rigs.
Also coming in above forecasts were Reading & Bates Inc and Global Marine Inc, but the biggest surprise came when Ensco International Inc reported on Wednesday.
Ensco's earnings per share rose to a record $0.74 against expectations of $0.66 and $0.34 a year ago.
Oppenheimer & Co analyst Carol Lau riased her 1997 and 1998 earnings estimates for Ensco on the back of the 164 percent rise in earnings per share from the year-ago period.

"With the largest fleet of premium jackup rigs in the world, we believe that Ensco is poised to produce double-digit growth through the sustained industry upcycle we expect over the next five to ten years," she said.
Ensco said that dayrates for its Gulf of Mexico jackup drilling rigs have increased by 17 percent to $48,000 from the first quarter.

One issue that has troubled the industry and the stockmarket is the possibilty that rig owners will take advantage of rising demand, high prices and tight supply to build rigs and eventually bust the boom.

Earlier this year, some stocks crashed when an unlisted shipping company said that it planned to build some new supply ships for the offshore oil industry and some analysts were quick to read that as an indication that the drilling sector would see a series of new builds.
However, the companies and most analysts say that the industry was stung so badly in the last building frenzy and downturn in the 1980s that it is much more conservative now.

"We have seen some speculative building but not a great deal and in the offshore sector especially, there is nothing to upset the supply/demand balance for the next two to three years," said Mark Urness, analyst at Salomon Brothers.
Ensco chief executive said that his company would build new rigs to fulfill prearranged contracts, but said that even at current levels, dayrates are not sufficient to justify new construction.
He said that to build a 350 foot Gulf of Mexico jackup would cost some $85-$90 million, while a 300 foot North Sea rig would cost $120-$140 million, and specialist rigs a great deal more.

Investors are also coming to realise that earnings in the sector are not directly tied to the oil price, although analysts say that perceptions of individual stocks are still tied to what happens in the crude market.

"If oil prices fall to $16-$17, then there will be an impact on investor perceptions of the sector," said Salomon's Urness, "but unless that continues for a prolonged period of time, it is unlikely to affect corporate earnings." ((-- David Chance New York Newsroom 212 859 1902))
